insight.title: Penguin Huddles Move in Waves to Share Heat
insight.subtitle: Emperor penguins use subtle dynamic ripples to ensure every member of the colony gets equal warmth.
insight.notificationHook: Penguins share heat using dynamic waves

sections.text: In freezing Antarctic blizzards, thousands of emperor penguins pack tightly together. Yet no individual remains trapped in the icy outer ring or suffocated at the center for long.

The entire huddle moves in continuous, microscopic waves. Every thirty seconds, a single penguin takes a small step, causing a gentle ripple that slowly shifts the entire group around the central warmth.
Without leaders or conflict, this fluid dynamic distributes heat perfectly across the colony. Every individual spends equal time sheltered in the core, cutting energy consumption in half.
Microscopic steps transform thousands of individuals into a single self-heating superorganism.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Russia launched missiles and drones across Ukraine overnight, killing at least six people. Russian President Vladimir Putin had promised a painful response after Ukraine hit the Crimean bridge. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said three people died and fifteen were wounded in Kyiv. The governor of Lviv reported two deaths at a train station. Another person died in the southern Zaporizhzhia region. Strikes knocked out power in parts of Kyiv and hit three bridges over the Dnipro river. Russia said its attack targeted military-industrial sites and transport infrastructure. Satellite images showed earlier Ukrainian strikes cut the highway on the nineteen-kilometer Crimean bridge in two. Putin had just met US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China.

Next, Japan reported core consumer inflation rose to two point two percent in October twenty twenty-six. Higher energy costs drove prices up after household energy subsidies ended in September. Government data shows gas prices jumped five point eight percent compared to September. Headline inflation, which includes food and energy, rose to two point three percent. After the report, Japan's Nikkei two two five stock index fell two point one percent. Japan has approved reintroducing energy subsidies in December to help households with high import costs. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament the central bank is watching the weak yen. Ma Tieying, an economist at DBS Group Research, expects the Bank of Japan to raise rates in December.

In technology news, California issued an investigative subpoena to AI chip maker Nvidia. State Attorney General Rob Bonta is investigating whether Nvidia or its former chief executive misled investors. Bonta said the state is checking if China received advanced chips or confidential information. Former chief executive officer Jensen Huang left the company last week after acknowledging extramarital affairs. Reports linked Huang to an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company and Nvidia customer. Some US lawmakers asked the Department of Commerce to check if Megaspeed sent Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia shares have dropped twenty-two percent since early November. Board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia has no plans to bring Huang back to the company.

Moving to cybersecurity, hackers may have accessed customer data from major financial institutions. JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard announced Thursday that a ransomware group breached a third-party vendor. The firms said the hackers reached third-party systems used by the companies. The attack may have exposed data from thousands of customers.

In health news, a new study showed a malaria antibody can weaken the effect of a malaria vaccine. Researchers tested the antibody, called L9LS, in infants in Mali. The antibody was seventy-eight percent effective at preventing malaria over a six-month season. However, it also reduced antibody levels produced by the R21 malaria vaccine by twenty to thirty percent. Both the antibody and the vaccine attach to the same protein on the malaria parasite. Robert Seder of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases said researchers will shift focus to other groups. Future studies will test the antibody in pregnant women and hospitalized children instead of infants. Researchers hope to start pivotal trials for the antibody in twenty twenty-eight.

Turning to shipping, internal emails show a US maritime agency warned that the American blockade of Iran raised costs. The US Maritime Administration warned that merchant ships face military attacks from both sides in the Gulf. Agency chief Stephen Carmel sent the alert in October after US forces disabled a Panama-flagged cargo ship. Official Michael Yarrington noted that war-risk insurance premiums were rising for commercial vessels. Al Jazeera obtained the internal documents through a Freedom of Information Act request. The International Maritime Organization reported at least twenty-five seafarers have died in regional vessel attacks since February. President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the United States controls the Strait of Hormuz.

Up next, the trade deal between Britain and India faces a test over Scotch whisky import taxes.

Trade talks between Britain and India have hit roadblocks over liquor tariffs. In the global spirits markets, while the United States, Europe, and China face volume contraction, India will add nearly 100 million consumers in the next five years.

Meta is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence boom. Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, shared the update in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes. In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement. Data centres globally used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, and that could nearly double by twenty thirty, according to the International Energy Agency.

Up to 100,000 young people from the European Union would be allowed to travel, work and study in the United Kingdom per year under a new youth mobility scheme. The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. In 2024, the European Union proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years. An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the European Union, which the government argues could add five billion pounds to the economy.

Turning to technology, US semiconductor equipment maker KLA opened an expanded plant in Singapore and announced plans for a third phase of expansion. The expanded site, Building 22B in Ang Mo Kio, gives the company about 210,000 square feet of new operational space. KLA, which makes machines and tools like surface profilers and testers, established its presence in Singapore in 1996 and began manufacturing there in 2006. In the longer term, the new spaces are expected to support about 1,000 new jobs across research and development and manufacturing engineering. KLA chief financial officer Bren Higgins said over 2,200 employees now work across multiple shifts. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore accounts for around one-fifth of global production for semiconductor equipment. Singapore is committing 800 million dollars under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan to the RIE Flagship in Semiconductors.

South Korea's Supreme Court overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for aiding in the declaration of martial law in December twenty twenty-four. The court overturned a 15-year prison sentence, sending the case back to the Seoul High Court for a retry. The 2024 decree was issued by the president at the time, Yoon Suk Yeol, and plunged the country into chaos for approximately six hours.

In education news, a new Harvard study suggests school cellphone restrictions boost students' learning. Students in schools that banned cellphones using lockable pouches gained the equivalent of one to two weeks of additional learning a year. About 77 percent of public schools had a policy prohibiting cellphones during class by the 2024-25 school year, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The study's authors analyzed test scores from millions of students across 4,600 schools. Some 800 of those schools required students to store phones in lockable pouches during the day, while 3,800 had no ban.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

In freezing Antarctic blizzards, thousands of emperor penguins pack tightly together. Yet no individual remains trapped in the icy outer ring or suffocated at the center for long. The entire huddle moves in continuous, microscopic waves. Every thirty seconds, a single penguin takes a small step, causing a gentle ripple that slowly shifts the entire group around the central warmth. Without leaders or conflict, this fluid dynamic distributes heat perfectly across the colony. Every individual spends equal time sheltered in the core, cutting energy consumption in half. Microscopic steps transform thousands of individuals into a single self-heating superorganism. How might your own team find a way to share the load without anyone ever taking charge?

Thank you for listening to this edition of the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. Today we bring you full context on three major world stories.

Why did Russia launch a large attack on Ukrainian cities overnight? Russian forces hit Ukrainian transport bridges and power lines after Ukraine damaged a strategic bridge. 

Let us look back at how this war began. In twenty fourteen, Russia took the Crimean peninsula from Ukraine by force. Moscow built a twelve mile bridge to connect Russia to Crimea in twenty eighteen. Russia used the peninsula as a military base. It stored weapons, troops, and air defense stockpiles there. In twenty twenty-two, Russia launched a full invasion of Ukraine. The war has killed hundreds of thousands of people. It forced millions of people to leave their homes. Ukraine wants all its land back. It sees the Crimean bridge as a symbol of Russian control. Ukraine also says the bridge carries military supplies to enemy troops. This week, Ukraine launched a seven stage attack using Neptune missiles and drones. The strike collapsed a two hundred meter road section into the sea. Ukraine said the strike saves lives by stopping supply trucks. Russia claimed the bridge was only used for civilian traffic. 

What changed the situation happened at a summit in China. Russian President Vladimir Putin met United States President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. He promised a far more painful response for the bridge attack. 

Hours later, Russia fired dozens of missiles and drones across Ukraine. In Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least three people died and fifteen were wounded. Two people died at a train station near Lviv. Another person died in the southern Zaporizhzhia region. Strikes hit three bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv. Electricity went out in parts of the capital city. Austrian, Brazilian, and Dutch embassies suffered light damage. Russia confirmed hitting military and transport sites. Russia said it shot down three hundred ten Ukrainian drones. Moscow-installed officials reported three people died in occupied eastern Ukraine. 

Why is this happening right now? Russia is stepping up attacks ahead of winter. Moscow also wants to show strength during peace talks. 

Talks led by the United States have shown little progress. Putin wants European security rules rewritten before ending the war. He wants NATO forces reduced in central and eastern Europe. He invited Europeans to Moscow for talks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called visiting Moscow a mistake. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe must join future negotiations. Watch to see if peace talks include European leaders soon.

Now, let us look at global money news in Asia.

Why did core inflation in Japan reach its highest level this year? Government energy discounts ended, so consumer utility bills went up.

To understand this story, we must look at how Japan handles energy. Japan buys most of its fuel from other countries. When global oil prices go up, living costs in Japan rise too. Recently, war in Iran pushed global fuel prices higher. Higher energy costs began to hurt Japanese families and businesses. To help citizens, Japan's government paid subsidies to lower household energy bills. These subsidies kept gas and electric bills lower for months.

What changed was the end of that official financial help. The energy subsidies expired at the end of September. That left consumers paying full market prices in October.

Government data showed core inflation rose to two point two percent in October twenty twenty-six. That was up from two point one percent in September. Core inflation leaves out fresh food prices. Overall headline inflation rose to two point three percent. Energy prices jumped two point two percent after falling in September. Gas prices jumped five point eight percent compared to the prior month. Fuel, light, and water charges rose three point four percent. Meanwhile, core-core inflation, which excludes food and energy, dropped slightly to two point two percent. After the report, Japan's Nikkei two twenty-five stock index fell two point one percent. The yen traded at one hundred fifty-nine point fifty-nine against the dollar.

Why did prices jump right now? Ending the subsidies pushed hidden energy costs straight onto monthly bills.

Wages have also grown above three percent for nine months in a row. Senior economist Ma Tieying from DBS Group Research said higher wages support underlying inflation. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda warned a weak yen could hurt household spending. Data shows a seventy-two percent chance the central bank raises rates in December. Japan approved plans to bring back energy subsidies in December. Economist Ma Tieying expects the central bank to raise interest rates three times by twenty twenty-seven. Watch to see if the central bank raises rates at its next meeting.

Next, we turn to a legal investigation in the American technology industry.

Why is California investigating computer chip maker Nvidia? State officials want to know if restricted technology secretly reached China.

Nvidia is a major technology company based in Santa Clara, California. It creates advanced chips used to build artificial intelligence tools. The United States government places strict limits on selling advanced chips to China. Officials do this to protect national security and military secrets. Under corporate law, public companies must be honest with investors about business risks.

What changed was a personal scandal involving Nvidia top leadership. Former chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to workplace affairs. One relationship was with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore firm called Megaspeed. Alice Huang is not related to Jensen Huang. United States lawmakers suspect Megaspeed may have sent Nvidia chips to China.

Today, California Attorney General Rob Bonta served Nvidia an investigative subpoena. He is checking if Nvidia or Jensen Huang broke state laws. Bonta said companies cannot mislead their investors about transnational risks. Megaspeed said claims about its supply chain are not supported by evidence. Nvidia shares dropped twenty-two percent over nine trading days after the news broke. Over seven weeks, the stock shed thirty-eight percent of its value. Board chair Harvey Jones said the company will not bring Jensen Huang back.

Why is this investigation happening right now? The chief executive's exit pushed state officials to inspect company records.

This probe could result in legal consequences if Nvidia misled the public. Some members of Congress want federal commerce officials to open their own investigation. Watch to see if federal regulators join California in probing Nvidia's chip sales.

Now, let us turn to what to know after hackers target Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase.

Hackers breached a third-party vendor used by major financial institutions. JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard announced a ransomware group hacked third-party systems used by the firms. The group may have accessed data from thousands of customers. CBS News reporter Ann Berry provided details on the breach.

Now we turn to a new study on malaria prevention.

Can a single antibody shot protect babies from malaria without ruining their regular vaccines? A new study shows that a protective antibody lowers the immune response from a key malaria vaccine.

Malaria is a dangerous disease caused by a parasite. Mosquitoes spread the parasite when they bite people. The infection killed about six hundred ten thousand people in twenty twenty-four. The majority of those who died were children under five in sub-Saharan Africa. Public health officials face tough choices because funding for malaria treatment is limited. Scientists made history by creating two vaccines called R twenty-one and RTS,S. These are the very first vaccines against any parasite. They provide protection for years. However, babies must receive several doses starting at five months of age. Giving children monthly pills is cheap, but parents sometimes struggle to give every dose. Scientists also created a laboratory protein called a monoclonal antibody. One shot of an antibody provides protection for several months. Kassoum Kayentao from a university in Mali said one shot lasts through a six-month malaria season. Officials hoped an antibody could protect newborn babies until they were old enough for vaccines. The main drawback is that antibodies are currently expensive to produce.

Scientists recently ran a study in Mali to test an antibody called L9LS on infants. They gave babies the antibody or a dummy shot called a placebo. After that, the babies received their standard doses of the R twenty-one vaccine.

The trial showed L9LS was seventy-eight percent effective at preventing malaria over six months. However, researchers reported that the shot caused a twenty to thirty percent drop in vaccine antibodies. Blood tests showed lower antibody levels, but real-world protection remains unclear. The vaccine trains the immune system to spot a specific parasite protein. The antibody L9LS binds to that exact same protein. Because of that, the antibody attached to the vaccine itself. That interference reduced the full immune response the vaccine was designed to build.

Researchers presented these blood test results at an annual tropical medicine conference. They wanted to explain why this specific order of treatments caused immune interference.

Scientists will now pause tests on babies and focus on other vulnerable groups. Robert Seder of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases said trials could resume later. Researchers hope to start pivotal studies for drug approval in twenty twenty-eight. The antibody could still help pregnant people and kids leaving the hospital after severe infections. Those recovering children face high risks from anemia after leaving the hospital. André-Marie Tchouatieu of Medicines for Malaria Venture said every safe tool still has a valuable role. He co-authored a review in the New England Journal of Medicine about malaria strategies.

Turning now to international affairs, an internal document details warnings given to United States officials.

Did the United States government know its naval blockade of Iran would raise global shipping costs? An internal memo reveals a maritime agency warned that military actions were driving up insurance rates.

The United States and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on February twenty-eighth. That event started a broader war and created chaos for global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway vital for transporting oil around the world. Since the conflict began, official reports record about one hundred thirty attacks on ships in the region. Those attacks resulted in the deaths of at least twenty-five seafarers. The United States Military Central Command enforced a blockade to stop ships from helping Iran. Military forces disabled or destroyed at least two dozen vessels linked to Iran. Most attacks were blamed on Iran, but American enforcement added new risks for merchant vessels. Insurance costs for ships began rising dramatically as the danger spread across the region. Insurance rates jumped from less than one percent of a vessel's value to over seven percent. These higher shipping costs caused global crude oil prices to surge up to sixty percent. Fertilizer prices also jumped by as much as one hundred twelve percent.

An internal email alert from October twelfth was recently released through a public records request. The memo showed officials recognized that military actions were creating economic fallout.

Stephen M Carmel led the United States Maritime Administration when he sent the internal alert. He emailed colleague Michael Yarrington after military forces disabled a Panama-flagged cargo ship named Ocean Molica. The ship had attempted to breach the blockade. Carmel noted that merchant ships faced physical attacks from both sides of the conflict. He warned this threat spread to nearby anchorages and the Gulf of Oman. Yarrington replied with news reports showing sharp spikes in war-risk insurance premiums. The memo warned that higher risks could lead to crew refusals and fewer available oil tankers. The agency sits under the Department of Transportation and promotes the domestic maritime industry.

These internal documents emerged because Al Jazeera submitted a Freedom of Information Act request. The news outlet obtained the records while peace talks between Washington and Tehran remained stalled.

This news shows some officials may have ignored economic warnings while enforcing the blockade. Former Navy Captain Todd Huntley said officials likely overlooked these predictable shipping risks. Maritime expert Ian Ralby said President Donald Trump appeared unconcerned by global economic fallout. Trump recently posted on social media that the United States controls Iran's money and the strait. High fuel costs contributed to heavy Republican losses in the November third midterm elections. Democrats gained control of fifty-six Senate seats and at least two hundred fifty-seven House seats. Observers will watch whether rising shipping costs force changes in future military blockades.

Next, a United Kingdom trade deal with India faces a stiff test over Scotch whisky import taxes.

Trade talks between Britain and India hit roadblocks over liquor tariffs. Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. Spirits markets in the United States, Europe, and China are shrinking. But India will add nearly one hundred million consumers in the next five years. That makes India a key market for liquor sellers.

Now we turn to tech news and corporate climate goals.

Why is Meta rethinking its goal to hit net-zero carbon emissions by twenty thirty? The company says running powerful artificial intelligence systems takes much more energy than expected.

In twenty twenty, Meta set a goal to reach net-zero carbon emissions by twenty thirty. Net zero means cutting greenhouse emissions as much as possible. Any leftover pollution is balanced out by paying for carbon removal projects. Meta aimed to align with the Paris Agreement to limit global warming. Back then, companies expected clean energy costs to fall steadily. However, building big artificial intelligence tools required massive new computer centers. These computing facilities use vast amounts of electricity. A study showed four hundred three top data centers used two percent of American electricity. Globally, data centers used four hundred fifteen terawatt hours of power in twenty twenty-four. That was about one point five percent of world energy supply. The International Energy Agency says that demand could nearly double by twenty thirty. Other large companies like Google, General Motors, and Walmart have also missed or lowered climate goals.

Meta began spending heavily on giant computer centers to power its new artificial intelligence tools. These new data centers caused the company's pollution levels to jump sharply.

Meta executives Rachel Peterson and Blair Swedeen shared the update in Meta's annual sustainability report. They wrote that Meta is re-evaluating its timeline for its twenty thirty net-zero goal. Meta reported that its net carbon emissions rose forty-five percent in twenty twenty-five. Total emissions reached eleven point eight million tonnes. Climate advocates view Meta's accounting methods for those figures with skepticism. Meanwhile, Meta announced a nine billion dollar data center project in Alberta, Canada. Canada is trying to attract these projects while local opposition grows in the United States. American voters passed forty local ballot initiatives this month to limit data centers. Businessman Kevin O'Leary planned a huge off-grid data center project called Wonder Valley in Alberta. He also planned a similar site in Utah, but residents there fiercely opposed it. Indigenous groups and Canadian residents have also started protesting and suing over environmental concerns. Hundreds of protesters recently gathered in Nova Scotia against a proposed data center for tech giant Anthropic.

Meta is pushing forward with artificial intelligence to keep up with industry rivals. The company says it cannot build required infrastructure while keeping its old climate timeline.

This change means tech expansion could slow down global progress on climate change. Looking ahead, governments may set new rules on where data centers can be built. Alberta's government has already proposed legislation to restrict future data center locations. It remains possible that public pushback against energy use could limit tech growth in the future.

Now let us turn to new agreements across the European continent.

Why are Britain and the European Union working on a new deal for young travelers? The two sides plan to let up to one hundred thousand young people travel abroad each year.

A decade ago, Britain voted to leave the European Union in a process known as Brexit. That vote ended free movement between Britain and twenty-seven European countries. After the split, trade checks increased and rules became much stricter. Young people lost the right to easily move, study, or work across the border. In twenty twenty-four, the European Union suggested a new youth travel plan. The British Labour party initially rejected that proposal while in opposition. Officials argued it looked too much like bringing back free movement. Over time, both sides recognized a need for closer ties due to global challenges. These challenges include war in Ukraine, US trade tariffs, and Chinese control of critical minerals. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated Britain lost more than it gained from leaving the bloc. He began pushing for a reset in relations with Europe.

Leaders met in Brussels for a summit to repair trade and travel ties. Negotiators worked down to the wire on Thursday to finalize a broad package of agreements.

Under the new plan, up to one hundred thousand young Britons can work or study in Europe. They can stay for up to three years under the proposed scheme. An equal number of young Europeans can do the same in Britain each year. The summit also produced a major agreement on food trade rules. That food deal removes paperwork for selling items like sausages and seeds across borders. Britain estimates the food plan could add five point one billion pounds a year to its economy. Another deal links carbon emission pricing to protect steel makers from extra taxes. However, differences remain over university tuition fees for European students. EU countries want domestic tuition rates, but Britain prefers offering only significantly reduced fees. Political opponents in Britain, including Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, criticized the agreements. Farage called the deal a very expensive error without a democratic mandate. Opponents argue the deals reopen Brexit divisions and force Britain to follow European rules.

Prime Minister Burnham wants to lower food prices for British shoppers and cut red tape for business. He also wants closer cooperation on European law enforcement and border security.

This agreement could make traveling and studying abroad much easier for young people. It may also lower grocery prices for British households over time. Looking ahead, the government plans to introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
